summary: In this episode of Work Reimagined, host Sarah Johnson talks with guest Mark Rivera about what remote work really looks like in 2025 and beyond, moving past the hype to the practices that make it work. Mark challenges the common idea that remote work simply means working from anywhere. He argues it is really about an async-first culture, documentation, and autonomy, supported by structured processes and trust. To show how companies build that culture, Mark points to GitLab, Automattic, and Doist, which have written handbooks for everything so employees can find answers without constant guidance. Asked whether this approach scales down, he says even small teams benefit from clear documentation because it reduces context-switching and keeps knowledge from being siloed. On tools, Mark cautions that Zoom and Slack help but are not the solution; culture is. Relying on Slack for everything, he warns, leads to burnout. For measuring productivity without micromanaging, he recommends focusing on outcomes over hours: setting goals, tracking progress on deliverables, and trusting the team, with transparency mattering more than check-ins. The conversation also tackles loneliness, a frequently cited downside of remote work. Mark suggests virtual coffee chats, occasional in-person retreats, and team rituals, stressing that remote does not have to mean isolated but does require intention. Looking ahead, he predicts remote-first companies will dominate talent acquisition, local offices may become optional hubs, and async culture will become standard practice. His closing advice for teams transitioning to remote work: focus on documentation, set clear goals, invest in culture, and trust your team.
takeaways: Treat remote work as an operating model built on async-first culture, documentation, autonomy, and trust, not just a change of location.
Write handbooks and clear documentation so people can find answers on their own; this helps small teams too by reducing context-switching and knowledge silos.
Tools like Zoom and Slack support remote work but don't replace culture, and relying on Slack for everything can burn people out.
Measure productivity by outcomes rather than hours: set goals, track deliverables, and favor transparency over frequent check-ins.
Fight isolation intentionally with virtual coffee chats, occasional in-person retreats, and team rituals.

claims.reasoning: All three companies keep large handbooks that are still in use. GitLab has a public handbook of over 2,000 pages covering 'nearly every aspect' of the company. Automattic's Field Guide is its employee handbook, covering 'everything from setting up a home office' to style guides. Doist has a company handbook of about 1,800 pages, described in a January 2026 post and a June 2026 article. 'For everything' is spoken hyperbole, but it matches how the companies describe their own handbooks. Note that Automattic's and Doist's handbooks are mainly internal; only parts are public. All sources are web results, mostly from the companies themselves; none came from the knowledge base.
